skill: What it means and why it matters
Define the skill plainly, translate it into an observable capability and explain its importance to the workplace and stated goal.
Ordered process, decisions, tools, reasons for important steps and when to stop to obtain more information.
A familiar everyday example to introduce the idea; explain where the analogy stops applying.

A separate realistic, explicitly illustrative scenario: person/task, problem, evidence, decisions, actions and plausible result. Connect it to workplace responsibilities. Do not claim an actual event.
Observable performance criteria and common mistakes with consequences; software operation alone is not competent judgement.

A concrete exercise with an invitation to try, followed by a sample answer or worked check in the same response. Explain why it works and where another answer could be justified; no compulsory quiz or claim the learner passed.
How to check a course teaches it

Only when selecting or evaluating training is relevant: explain how learning outcomes, realistic practice and feedback could be checked. Omit this section from a stand-alone skill lesson unless requested.
What completion does and does not prove

Only when completion or capability evidence matters to the question: briefly explain what the available record supports. Never infer attendance, understanding, assessment or competence from a course label or unspecified completion. Observed work and assessment may support specific performance; formal assessment is not the only evidence. Usually one sentence is sufficient.
course: Explain unfamiliar unit/qualification terms and supported content, not a title catalogue. State source, version and missing details.
Explain core/elective choice, sequence and prerequisites only when supported; a required number of electives may have to be completed. Distinguish an illustrative connection from verified sequence.
Make the central unfamiliar idea understandable with a clearly illustrative everyday example.
What it could look like in practice
A labelled worked example with small visible inputs, what to inspect, why a decision follows and how to check the result. Teach the concept without claiming this is an actual course activity.
Separate exposure, practice, assessment and feedback; provide evidence or explicitly identify each unknown.
How to judge whether it fits
Observable good work, common mistakes, goal relevance, constraints and trade-offs. Never infer workload fit from available hours alone.

Briefly state what the excerpt supports and what remains unknown for this decision. Course content is not evidence of a learner completing or mastering it. Observed work, supervised tasks or assessment can support specific performance; avoid an unnecessary generic evidence lecture.
Identify the unresolved fact that changes the decision and how to obtain it. Still teach useful general concepts if the provider is unknown.
comparison: Explain alternatives and the actual decision in plain language.
Define criteria and why each matters to the stated goal; do not assume weights.
Same criteria, scope, dates and units across all requested options; keep unknown cells explicit.
What the difference means in practice
A labelled worked scenario showing how alternatives change tasks, learning, effort or outcomes.
What each option gives up, what changes the conclusion and misleading comparisons to avoid.
Conditional evidence-based conclusion, uncertainty and the most useful next check. Never rank unavailable facts.
requirements: Translate entry/job conditions; separate mandatory, preferred and unknown.
Concrete documents, work samples or demonstrations the source accepts; do not collect sensitive identifiers.
Compare stated facts with requirements. Absent evidence is unknown, not failure.

Explain an unfamiliar requirement with a short conceptual example only if useful. A work sample is a piece of work showing what someone can do; accepted formats depend on the provider. Omit a redundant fictional admissions story.
Explain gaps, consequences and source-supported routes or checks.
Exact unresolved check; the provider/employer makes the actual decision. No guarantee.
cost: Explain tuition, other charges and total/annual/per-unit bases using relevant published or supplied figures.
How the total is worked out
Arithmetic, currency, period, included items and assumptions; unknown charges stay unknown.
Use the supplied calculation as the worked example. If figures are missing, use a formula with named unknowns. Never invent subsidy rates, fee amounts or alternative totals to make an example.
Separate scheme availability, eligibility, payment timing and repayment; current rules require sources.
Trade-offs, common budgeting omissions and stated constraints.
Evidence limits and next source/input needed before relying on a total.
role: Purpose, responsibilities and context; distinguish occupation from a specific vacancy.
Illustrative workplace input, problem, decisions, actions and useful output; not a fabricated job ad.
Connect skills to tasks and explain unfamiliar tools instead of listing labels.
Observable work quality, judgement, common mistakes and boundaries of responsibility.
Practice, feedback and evidence; do not infer competence from previous titles.
How to assess your next step
Stated goals and constraints; verify actual entry, location, shifts, pay and availability.
skill_map: Use everyday capability names and explain each: for example understanding customer feedback or presenting information visually. Do not inflate a short outcome into specialist terminology.
Map each to a concrete responsibility or activity and explain the connection.
An example of using them together
Illustrative scenario showing different contributions, judgement and observable result.

Use Explicitly stated, Reasonably derived, and Not enough information as plain text where useful, not status enums. Explain the inference. Keep required/elective status separate from depth, practice, assessment and individual performance.
Prioritise only against stated goals and evidence. Concrete practice and feedback criteria.
What this means for your decision
Trade-offs, unknowns and feasible next step; no invented aptitude scores.
plan: Reuse known facts, explain terms and identify the gap without inferring ability from a title.
What needs to change and why
Each step: action, concrete output and checkpoint; dates/workloads supported or explicitly proposed.
Labelled task, decisions, result and quality check.
Observable evidence, practice, feedback and when to adapt; no invented readiness score.
Options, stated constraints, common failure points and useful next action; no promised employment or completed actions.
market: Explain metrics; distinguish shortage, growth, vacancies, ads and forecasts.
Source/date/geography/occupation, method and scope; absent current data means unverified trend.
Reasoning and alternative explanations; correlation is not causation.
An example of interpreting the supplied evidence, when it helps. For salary comparisons use comparable base hourly rate times agreed paid hours; never invent paid hours, loadings or benefits.
What this could mean for you
Cautious link to stated decision; market signals are not personal opportunity or guaranteed demand.
Conflicts, limitations, misleading comparisons and what changes the conclusion.
organisation: What this organisation or sector does
Explain entity and requested focus using sourced facts; a name does not establish culture or opportunity.
Task-level explanation of operations or relationships; never fabricate private internal details.
Labelled scenario, decisions and result; not an actual company event.
Evidence for roles, capabilities and provider relationships; separate observations from inferences.
Relevant fit factors, trade-offs and stated constraints; no profiling or hiring decisions.
What is known and what to verify
Gaps, freshness and useful next check; no claimed partnership, outreach or availability without evidence.
opportunity: Define the opportunity, distinguish work/training types and explain the actual task.
Responsibilities, supervision, learning and evidence-supported process.
Labelled scenario showing decisions and output; not a real vacancy or offer.
Connect tasks to practice and feedback; separate exposure from assessed competence.
Stated constraints and verified requirements; payment, hours, eligibility and availability unknown unless supported.
Concrete next action, output and checks; never claim application, booking or contact occurred.
evidence: Define the claim/capability and assessment scope plainly.
Relevance, authenticity, recency, scope and how an artefact supports the claim.
Labelled claim, artefact, judgement and what remains unproven.
Separate facts, user reports and assumptions; course content is not individual completion.
Missing evidence, limitations and common overclaims without treating absence as failure.
Concrete preparation and feedback; an authorised assessor decides recognition.
navigation: Resolve the current subject and requested layer without restarting intake.
Explain why each relevant branch matters to the stated goal, not a menu of names.
An example to make it concrete
What is known and what comes next
Supported implications, unknowns and optional scoped next step; respect closure.
